title: Samvat 2082 Ends in Red: 83 Large-Caps Fall Up to 60% as Small-Caps Mint Multibaggers
excerpt: India's benchmark Nifty fell about 11 percent over Samvat 2082, with 83 large-cap stocks losing ground — some by up to 60 percent — while 60 small-cap stocks more than doubled, an Economic Times analysis of the year since last Diwali shows.
body:
• Samvat 2082 was a losing year for India's blue chips: the Nifty 50 fell about 11 percent since last Diwali, 83 large-cap stocks declined and only 43 gained, according to an Economic Times analysis.
  • The worst large-cap falls ran to 60 percent, even as 60 small-cap stocks delivered multibagger returns above 100 percent — the top gainers rose as much as 650 percent, led by pharmaceutical, defence and engineering names.
  • Large-cap mutual funds fell an average of 9.34 percent over the same period, so most diversified India portfolios held by NRI investors shrank too.
  • Strategists blame high oil prices, slowing liquidity and geopolitical risk; the India VIX above 30 signals traders expect the swings to continue into the new Samvat.

Investors who bought India's biggest companies at last Diwali's Muhurat session are closing Samvat 2082 with losses. An analysis by market data compiled for The Economic Times shows the Nifty 50 down about 11 percent over the Samvat year, with 83 large-cap stocks in the red — the steepest falls approaching 60 percent — against only 43 gainers. It is the weakest Samvat for the benchmark in more than a decade.

Two markets in one year

The pain at the top coexisted with exuberance at the bottom. Sixty small-cap stocks more than doubled over the year, with the best performers gaining as much as 650 percent, concentrated in pharmaceutical, defence and engineering shares. That split — falling blue chips, soaring small caps — is the reverse of the usual risk pattern, in which large caps hold up better in a downturn. For fund investors the large-cap experience was broadly negative: ET Mutual Funds data show large-cap funds lost an average of 9.34 percent since last Diwali, with the worst fund down about 13.2 percent and even the largest fund in the category, ICICI Prudential Large Cap, down 11.39 percent. Small-cap funds were the only major equity category in positive territory on average.

Why blue chips fell

The year's drivers were macro, not company-specific: crude oil prices stayed high, domestic liquidity tightened, and geopolitical risk kept foreign investors cautious. Global asset managers including BlackRock have stayed underweight on Indian equities despite the lower prices, arguing that valuations still run ahead of earnings growth — a "valuation trap" in which cheap-looking stocks get cheaper as profit forecasts fall. The India VIX, the market's fear gauge, has climbed above 30, a level that signals expectations of large swings.

What it means for your portfolio

For diaspora investors holding India exposure through large-cap funds or direct blue-chip holdings, Samvat 2082 is a reminder that a falling index does not automatically make large caps the safe corner of the market — this year the losses were broad, with more than two-thirds of large-cap stocks declining. Advisers quoted in the ET Mutual Funds analysis continue to favour gradual, SIP-based entry over lump sums, a long horizon, and keeping small caps — this year's winners — as a limited share of an equity portfolio rather than its core, given how concentrated the multibagger gains were. The new Samvat opens with earnings season as the first test: strategists say a durable turn needs profit growth, not just lower prices.
